samples.summary: The printed copy-paste URL is single-use, so the "visit the URL above" fallback can already be spent (and any non-GET/duplicate hit spends it)
samples.evidence: `console.error(`Opening browser: ${startUrl}`)` followed by `console.error('If the browser does not open, visit the URL above.')` prints `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/start`, but the `/start` handler (lines 266-281) sets `startConsumed = true` on the *first request of any method* — there is no `req.method` check, so a HEAD/OPTIONS probe, a browser reload, a back-navigation, an extension prefetch, or the browser having already followed it all leave the printed fallback URL answering `410 START_CONSUMED_MESSAGE`. Once that happens the login cannot be recovered; it only fails at the 30s timeout with the generic "Login timed out" message, which never mentions the consumed link. Previously the printed URL was the server authorize URL and was re-visitable.

samples.summary: Any local process can force the timeout to report the misleading version-skew message that nudges the user to `--allow-unbound-callback`
samples.evidence: `sawUnboundCallback` is set by *any* `GET /callback?code=…` with no `state` (line 306-316) — a request the surrounding comment itself says is "reachable by any local process or visited page". The timeout at line 373-382 then reports `UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE`, which tells the user the server is old and to re-run with `--allow-unbound-callback`. So the downgrade nudge the comment claims to have avoided is still reachable by an attacker; it is merely deferred to the timeout, and a genuine timeout (slow GitHub login) is then misdiagnosed as version skew.

samples.summary: The edited fail-safe test no longer exercises the empty-`WAFFLEBASE_CHANGED_AREAS` guard it documents — it short-circuits on the push-to-main branch
samples.evidence: `resolve()` (scripts/changed-areas.mjs:510) skips the env parsing on a falsy `WAFFLEBASE_CHANGED_AREAS` and then returns `FULL("push to main …")` at line 530-534 whenever `GITHUB_EVENT_NAME=push` and `GITHUB_REF_NAME=main`. By adding those two vars the test now always resolves via the push-to-main branch, so `out.full === true` would hold even if the empty-string handling regressed (e.g. started returning `{full:false,packages:[],tags:[]}`). The regression the comment above it describes is now untested; a fixture repo root or asserting on the classification path would be needed to keep the coverage.

samples.summary: `seg('')` turns an empty identifier into a thrown Error on paths that previously produced a request, and the throw is synchronous from `HttpClient` getters rather than a rejected promise
samples.evidence: `seg` throws for `''` and for `.`/`..`. `HttpClient.getDocument`/`getCell`/etc. build the path eagerly (http-client.ts:202, 355), so the throw is synchronous, not a rejected promise — a caller that does `client.getDocument(id).catch(...)` without a surrounding try/catch would now blow up instead of being caught. All in-tree call sites happen to `await` inside a try, but the contract change is easy to trip; consider returning a rejected promise or validating in `request()`.

samples.summary: A present-but-malformed `cliState` is only rejected when the port is also valid, so the 400 the doc promises is skipped on the invalid-port path
samples.evidence: `normalizeCliState(cliState)` is called inside the `Number.isInteger(portNum) && 1024<=port<=65535` block (lines 67-77). With `mode=cli` and an out-of-range port, an invalid `cliState` is silently ignored and the request falls through to the *web* flow — the guard sets auth cookies and redirects to `FRONTEND_URL` for what was clearly a CLI attempt, instead of the documented 400. The class doc says "A present-but-malformed nonce is a 400 … never a silent drop", which is not true on this path.

finding.summary: `GET /start` is single-use and method-agnostic, so any duplicate/speculative request silently breaks the login for 30s
finding.evidence: `if (startConsumed) { res.writeHead(410) … }` at login.ts:272-276 marks the redirect consumed on the *first* request of any kind, before the browser has necessarily navigated. Real, non-adversarial duplicates exist: (a) a HEAD/preview/URL-scanner request (the handler never checks `req.method`, so HEAD consumes it), (b) omnibox/link prefetch when the user copy-pastes the printed `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/start` — the very headless path the comment at login.ts:52-65 says must keep working, (c) the user reloading or hitting Back and retrying after a hiccup, (d) a browser launcher that issues the URL twice. In all of these the real navigation gets `410 START_CONSUMED_MESSAGE`, no `/callback` ever arrives, and the CLI blocks the full 30s (login.ts:373-385) before failing with the generic `Login timed out` — with no hint that the one-time link was burnt. The previous code passed the authorize URL directly to `open()` and had no such failure mode, so this is a newly introduced hang/regression on ordinary paths.

verdict.reason: Verified in the repository. The /start handler at login.ts:266-281 sets `startConsumed = true` on the first request of ANY method — `req.method` is never read anywhere in packages/cli/src (grep for req.method/method ===/HEAD returns zero matches), so a HEAD, prefetch, or scanner probe burns the one-time redirect and the user's real navigation receives 410 START_CONSUMED_MESSAGE (lines 272-276). The printed/opened URL is that same consumable /start (constructed line 399, printed line 67, passed to open() line 72), and the comment at lines 52-65 explicitly commits to it as the headless copy-paste path, so copy-paste, reload, and Back-then-retry all funnel through it. Once burnt, no /callback ever arrives, so waitForCallback() (line 80) blocks on callbackPromise, which only settles from /callback (line 369) or the setTimeout(..., 30_000) at lines 373-385 — and that timeout branch has no startConsumed arm, reporting only sawUnboundCallback ? UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE : 'Login timed out'. No refutation ground applies: the code matches the quoted lines (not not-present); there is no method check, no re-issue allowance, and no consumed-state detection at the timeout (not already-guarded); and a 30s block ending in a misleading generic error on ordinary user paths is squarely a mis-handled-failure/broken-invariant issue in the Correctness lane (not out-of-scope). The single-use property is intentional per lines 58-61, but that justifies rejecting a second hand-off, not consuming on a HEAD nor masking the cause as a plain timeout. One overstatement in the finding: the browser does render START_CONSUMED_MESSAGE, so the user gets a hint there — but the CLI side gives none and still blocks the full 30s.

finding.summary: `sawUnboundCallback` lets any local process (or visited page) control the CLI's final error message, producing a false version-skew report
finding.evidence: `sawUnboundCallback` is set at login.ts:309-310 by *any* `GET /callback?code=…` with no `state`, which the surrounding comment itself notes is 'reachable by any local process or visited page'. The timeout then reports `UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE` (login.ts:378-380) instead of 'Login timed out'. So a stray/hostile nonce-less request during an otherwise ordinary timeout (browser never finished, network hiccup) makes the CLI assert the *server* is out of date and instruct the user to re-run with `--allow-unbound-callback` — the exact downgrade steer the comment at login.ts:298-305 claims to have closed; it is merely deferred to the timeout. The error is factually wrong on a path where the server is perfectly current.

verdict.reason: The cited code exists as described: login.ts:306-317 sets sawUnboundCallback on any nonce-less /callback?code=..., and login.ts:373-385 substitutes UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE for the timeout message, so a stray/hostile request plus an ordinary timeout does produce the version-skew text. But it is not blocking under the correctness lens. (1) The entire effect is which of two error strings is used on an already-failing terminal path: both branches reject the same promise (login.ts:376-382), close() still runs in the caller's finally (login.ts:81-83), srv.close() runs unconditionally (login.ts:384), the exchange at login.ts:86 is never reached and saveSession (login.ts:168) is unreachable. No caller branches on the message text. So there is no crash, data loss, incorrect state update, resource leak, swallowed failure, or inverted condition - only diagnostic-message accuracy, nit/minor impact at most. (2) The behavior is the explicitly documented contract, not an oversight: docs/design/cli.md:229-237 specifies the nonce-less callback must NOT end the login and that the version-skew message replaces the timeout message when the 30 seconds expire having seen nothing else; docs/design/rest-api.md:380 records the same tradeoff, and packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts:92-119 pins it (line 104 deliberately keeps the flag out of the live warning). Implementation matches spec, so the objection is with the design tradeoff, owned by the architecture/design-fit lens. (3) The harm the finding rests on - an attacker-triggerable request steering the user toward --allow-unbound-callback and thereby disabling nonce binding - is a downgrade/attacker-influence concern owned by the security lens, explicitly out of this lane.
